    // The shortest rotation carrying `from` onto `to`, built from the half-way
    // vector so that no trigonometry appears. Exactly opposed inputs have no
    // shortest rotation — every half-turn about a perpendicular axis serves — and
    // one such axis is chosen rather than leaving the result undefined.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternions_and_spatial_rotation)
    RotationTo(from: Direction3D, to: Direction3D): Quaternion
    {
        var a = from.Vector;
        var b = to.Vector;
        var axis = a.Cross(b);
        var w = 1.0 + a.Dot(b);
        var perpendicular = a.X.Abs < 0.9 ? Vector3D(1.0, 0.0, 0.0).Cross(a) : Vector3D(0.0, 1.0, 0.0).Cross(a);
        return w <= 0.000001
            ? Quaternion(perpendicular.Normalize.X, perpendicular.Normalize.Y, perpendicular.Normalize.Z, 0.0)
            : Quaternion(axis.X, axis.Y, axis.Z, w).Normalize;
    }

    // The orientation whose local Z runs along `axis` — the principal frame of
    // every axially symmetric primitive here, and the orientation to give a
    // `SolverBody3D` built from a cylinder or a capsule.
    AxialOrientation(axis: Direction3D): Quaternion
        => RotationTo(Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 1.0).FromVectorUnchecked, axis);

    //==
    // # Solver bodies — impulse response
    //
    // Everything the solver needs to know about one body, and the reason
    // `SolverBody3D` stores an inverse inertia DIAGONAL rather than a tensor:
    // applying I^-1 is then a rotation into the principal frame, three multiplies,
    // and a rotation back, with no matrix to assemble and nothing to invert.

    // The dimensionless mobility of a motion kind: 1 for a body that responds to
    // impulses, 0 for one that does not. The single place in this library that
    // reads `BodyMotion`, so that the solver itself has no case analysis and no
    // branch a static body can take by accident.
    MobilityScale(motion: BodyMotion): Number
        => match (motion) {
            Static => 0.0;
            Kinematic => 0.0;
            Dynamic => 1.0;
        };

    // The component-wise product of two vectors: the diagonal matrix product that
    // applying a principal inertia amounts to.
    ComponentProduct(a: Vector3D, b: Vector3D): Vector3D
        => Vector3D(a.X * b.X, a.Y * b.Y, a.Z * b.Z);

    // The reciprocal of each principal moment, with a zero moment mapping to zero
    // rather than to infinity: a body with no inertia about an axis is one that
    // cannot be spun about it, which is what an immovable body means.
    InverseMoments(moments: Vector3D): Vector3D
        => Vector3D(
            moments.X > 0.0 ? 1.0 / moments.X : 0.0,
            moments.Y > 0.0 ? 1.0 / moments.Y : 0.0,
            moments.Z > 0.0 ? 1.0 / moments.Z : 0.0);

    // The angular velocity change an angular impulse (newton-meter-seconds, world
    // frame) produces: I^-1 L, taken through the body's principal frame.
    AngularResponse(self: SolverBody3D, angularImpulse: Vector3D): Vector3D
        => ComponentProduct(
                angularImpulse.Transform(self.Orientation.Inverse),
                self.InverseInertia)
            .Transform(self.Orientation);

    // The world velocity of the material point of the body currently at `point`:
    // the centre's velocity plus the rotation carried out to the lever arm.
    VelocityAt(self: SolverBody3D, point: Point3D): Vector3D
        => self.Velocity.Linear + self.Velocity.Angular.Cross(self.Center.Between(point));

    // The body after an impulse of `impulse` newton-seconds applied at world point
    // `point`. Position and orientation are untouched: an impulse changes velocity
    // only, and an immovable body changes not at all.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impulse_(physics))
    ApplyImpulse(self: SolverBody3D, impulse: Vector3D, point: Point3D): SolverBody3D
        => SolverBody3D(
            self.Center,
            self.Orientation,
            SpatialVelocity3D(
                self.Velocity.Linear + impulse * self.InverseMass,
                self.Velocity.Angular
                    + AngularResponse(self, self.Center.Between(point).Cross(impulse))),
            self.InverseMass,
            self.InverseInertia,
            self.LinearDamping,
            self.AngularDamping,
            self.GravityScale);

    // The body with a different twist and everything else left alone.
    WithVelocity(self: SolverBody3D, velocity: SpatialVelocity3D): SolverBody3D
        => SolverBody3D(self.Center, self.Orientation, velocity, self.InverseMass,
            self.InverseInertia, self.LinearDamping, self.AngularDamping, self.GravityScale);

    // The body at rest: the starting state of the position pass, where the twist
    // is a pseudo-velocity rather than a motion.
    AtRest(self: SolverBody3D): SolverBody3D
        => WithVelocity(self, SpatialVelocity3D(Vector3D.Zero, Vector3D.Zero));

    // The effective mass along `direction` for an impulse applied at `anchorA` on A
    // and at `anchorB` on B: the scalar that turns an impulse magnitude into the
    // relative speed change it buys, so the impulse needed for a wanted speed
    // change is that change divided by this. Made of the two inverse masses plus
    // what each body's rotation contributes through its own lever arm.
    // Precondition: `direction` is unit.
    //
    // The two anchors are separate because a JOINT holds two points that are
    // supposed to coincide and generally do not; a CONTACT is the special case
    // where both are the contact point.
    DirectionalMass(a: SolverBody3D, b: SolverBody3D, anchorA: Point3D, anchorB: Point3D,
        direction: Vector3D): Number
    {
        var ra = a.Center.Between(anchorA);
        var rb = b.Center.Between(anchorB);
        var angularA = AngularResponse(a, ra.Cross(direction)).Cross(ra);
        var angularB = AngularResponse(b, rb.Cross(direction)).Cross(rb);
        return a.InverseMass + b.InverseMass + direction.Dot(angularA + angularB);
    }

    // The effective mass of a contact, where both bodies are anchored at the same
    // world point.
    DirectionalMass(a: SolverBody3D, b: SolverBody3D, point: Point3D, direction: Vector3D): Number
        => DirectionalMass(a, b, point, point, direction);

    // The speed at which the two anchor points separate along `direction`: B's
    // material velocity at its anchor minus A's at its own.
    SeparationSpeed(a: SolverBody3D, b: SolverBody3D, anchorA: Point3D, anchorB: Point3D,
        direction: Vector3D): Number
        => (VelocityAt(b, anchorB) - VelocityAt(a, anchorA)).Dot(direction);

    // The speed at which the two bodies' material points at `point` separate along
    // `direction`. Negative along a contact normal means the pair is closing,
    // because the normal runs from A toward B.
    SeparationSpeed(a: SolverBody3D, b: SolverBody3D, point: Point3D, direction: Vector3D): Number
        => SeparationSpeed(a, b, point, point, direction);

    // The solver's view of an authored body, with its shape's principal moments
    // supplied by the caller (from `PrincipalMoments`) and its principal
    // orientation folded into the pose. A static or kinematic body loses both
    // inverses, which is the whole of how the solver knows not to move it.
    SolverBody(body: RigidBody3D, principalMoments: Vector3D): SolverBody3D
    {
        var mobility = MobilityScale(body.Motion);
        var mass = body.MassProperties.Mass.Amount;
        return SolverBody3D(
            body.Pose.Position + body.MassProperties.CenterOfMass.Offset.Transform(body.Pose.Orientation),
            body.Pose.Orientation,
            SpatialVelocity3D(body.LinearVelocity, body.AngularVelocity),
            mass > 0.0 ? mobility / mass : 0.0,
            InverseMoments(principalMoments) * mobility,
            body.LinearDamping,
            body.AngularDamping,
            body.GravityScale);
    }
